evidence_quotes.quote: We develop these arguments by focusing on the Water Users Association model in Lilongwe, Malawi.

Forty-eight semi-structured interviews were held with representatives of WaterAid (both at the headquarters in London and at the ofﬁce of the Country Programme in Malawi), as well as WUAs representatives and key informants involved in or knowledgeable about the WUAs. Focus group discussions were held with WUAs, Community-based Organizations and the local NGO partners. Opinions of local consumers were gathered through semi-structured questionnaires with 30 households in the area beneﬁting from the project.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 7, Water Supply Services in Lilongwe
evidence_quotes.quote: WaterAid Malawi’s intervention was targeted at reversing the rationing and kiosk disconnection policy.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 10, Implementing the Model: Context Specificity and Everyday Practices of Service Provision
evidence_quotes.quote: Furthermore, responses from the household survey suggest that the majority of the people living in the project area were unaware of both the elections of and application procedures for the Executive Committee.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 12, The Impact of Institutional Bricolage on Service Provision
evidence_quotes.quote: In 2014, the ratio of the price of the bulk water (MK 91/m3) and the ﬁnal price to consumers (MK 300/m3) had grown from 1:2.15 to 1:3.29. The high price charged at the kiosks to consumers is the result of a number of factors. As the WUA has to follow the principles of cost-recovery and proﬁt-making, all costs associated with the incorporation of the local elite in the WUA and the repayment of arrears automatically translate into higher prices at the kiosks.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 12, The Impact of Institutional Bricolage on Service Provision
evidence_quotes.quote: Last, despite the increase in price, the WUAs were hardly able to ensure improved service provision to their consumers: asset maintenance and continuity of the service remain of poor quality. In case of breakage, a response from the Lilongwe Water Board may take up to 3 months. The complex bureaucratic procedures adopted by the utility for the procurement of goods further slow down the simplest repair.

country.comment: Single-country urban/peri-urban case study in Lilongwe, Malawi.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF p. 5, Section 'Water Supply Services in Lilongwe'

effect_estimate.comment: Qualitative case study with descriptive administrative/tariff figures reported from WUA, KMU and WaterAid records; no statistical hypothesis tests or regression estimates reported.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Formalizing communal kiosk management into registered cooperative Water Users Associations (WUAs) across 6 low-income communities in peri-urban Lilongwe averted the utility's planned disconnection of 40% of operational kiosks and reduced accumulated arrears from MKW 30.5 million (January 2006) to MKW 14.5 million (January 2007), keeping water flowing; however, institutional bricolage and elite capture (co-optation of traditional chiefs, politicians and religious leaders onto WUA Boards and Executive Committees with monthly honoraria and allowances) drove kiosk retail water prices from MK 125/m3 vs MK 58/m3 bulk tariff (1:2.15 ratio in 2008–2009) to MK 300/m3 vs MK 91/m3 bulk tariff (1:3.29 ratio in 2014), excluded ordinary residents from participatory governance, and failed to improve maintenance or continuity (utility repairs taking up to 3 months, shortages lasting 2–3 days, and some areas receiving water only 2 days per week).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 7, Section 'Water Supply Services in Lilongwe'; PDF pp. 9–12, Sections 'Implementing the Model' and 'The Impact of Institutional Bricolage on Service Provision'; PDF p. 13, Conclusions

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by qualitative case study design (CASP); rated 2 because fieldwork across 2008–2009 and 2013–2014 directly observes and documents how WUA legal registration, service contracts, chief land/nomination discretion, elite board honoraria, arrears recovery rules and utility procurement procedures shape kiosk tariffs, disconnections and service continuity.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 2, Introduction; PDF pp. 8–12, Sections 'Designing the Model', 'Implementing the Model' and 'The Impact of Institutional Bricolage on Service Provision'; Tables 1–4, PDF pp. 8, 11

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines participatory WUA governance and elite capture (participation), chiefs' land control for kiosk siting (property) and discretionary selection of committee candidates (discretion), formal cooperative registration, candidate application rules and complex utility repair procurement (procedural_steps, delay), full-cost-recovery kiosk tariffs incorporating elite overhead and past debt (fees), planned utility kiosk disconnections for arrears/low volume (disconnection), KMU consumer complaint mediation (complaint) and co-optation of chiefs/MPs/NGO/utility actors (political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, participation, discretion, fees, disconnection, property, procedural_steps, delay, complaint, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 7–12, Sections 'Water Supply Services in Lilongwe', 'Designing the Model', 'Implementing the Model' and 'The Impact of Institutional Bricolage on Service Provision'
